::: {#rem-rarity-odds}
#### Rarity and odds

For an [event](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-event) $A$
with [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $p$,
the [odds](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-odds) in favour of $A$ are $p / (1 - p)$,
and the odds against $A$ are $(1 - p) / p$ [@grinstead1997introduction, Definition 1.4].
Let $r = 1/p$ be the [rarity](#def-rarity) of an [outcome](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-experiment-outcome) with probability $p$.
Then the odds against are $r - 1$.

```{r}
#| label: rarity-odds
p <- c(1 / 4, 1 / 100, 1)
rarity <- 1 / p
odds_against <- (1 - p) / p
rarity - odds_against
rarity
odds_against
```

The first printed line shows that the rarity exceeds the odds against by exactly $1$ for each $p$.
An event with probability $1/4$ has rarity $`r rarity[1]`$ and odds of $`r odds_against[1]`$ to $1$ against.
The two nearly agree for a small $p$.
At $p = 1$ the rarity is $`r rarity[3]`$ and the odds against are $`r odds_against[3]`$.

The odds compare an event with its
[complement](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-complement),
so they apply to an event and take values in $[0, \infty]$,
for a [continuous random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-continuous-rv) as well.
The rarity compares an
[outcome](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-experiment-outcome)
with the whole [sample space](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-sample-space).

:::
